strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem (decoding-time distribution drift in KV-cache retrieval) with a clear empirical demonstration of the phenomenon (Fig. 1) before proposing a fix.

The core technical idea—normalizing and randomly rotating queries/keys onto the unit hypersphere so that a fixed, data-independent set of sign-pattern centroids can be used instead of learned/stale centroids—is elegant and reasonably novel in the KV-retrieval context, and is partially theoretically justified via Proposition 4.1 (Beta-distribution priors for rotated subspace coordinates), which also motivates the quantization level design.

The system design is thorough: a two-stage coarse-to-fine pipeline (collision voting + calibrated low-bit reranking with an alpha-correction term to counteract quantization-induced underestimation of inner products), a sliding-window buffer for incremental re-indexing of new keys, and a UVA-based on-demand fetch mechanism to avoid explicit CPU-GPU memcpy overhead — this reflects genuine algorithm-system co-design.

Empirical results are extensive and consistently favorable: accuracy gains over MagicPIG/PQCache across multiple model families (Qwen3-4B/8B, DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B) and benchmarks (AIME25, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, LongBench-V2), together with substantial decoding latency/throughput improvements (up to 2.8x over full attention, 17x/44x over MagicPIG/PQCache at 1M tokens) and scaling to context lengths where full attention OOMs.

Ablations (Fig. 10, Section 5.3/5.4) isolate the contribution of the normalize-rotate-centroid design and the alpha-correction term, and provide some design-space characterization (candidate ratio vs KV length, multi-tier collision shaping).
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is limited to MagicPIG and PQCache; several more recent and highly relevant CPU-offloaded KV-retrieval systems mentioned in the related work (RetroInfer, ShadowKV, RetrievalAttention, Quest) are never empirically compared against, even though they target the same problem setting and some explicitly address CPU-GPU data movement, weakening the significance claims relative to true state of the art.

Reproducibility is limited: no code/artifact release is mentioned, several hyperparameters (e.g., B, m used in main experiments vs. the B=16,m=8 default in Section 5.4, adaptive (ρ,β) schedule specifics) are not fully specified for the main results tables, and baseline configuration choices (e.g., PQCache's 20% compression ratio) are asserted as 'paper-recommended' without justifying fairness of budget matching against ParisKV's fixed top-K=100.

Accuracy results (Table 2, 3) are reported without variance/error bars or multiple-seed evaluation, which is especially concerning for pass@8 on AIME25 (small sample size, high variance) and could make some of the large reported gaps (e.g., +76.7 points) less statistically robust than presented.

The complexity analysis (Section 4.3) is coarse and does not quantify the actual overhead of coarse-stage voting, reranking, and buffer maintenance kernels relative to end-to-end latency in a rigorous breakdown beyond Figure 6's qualitative kernel comparisons; there's limited analysis of how retrieval overhead scales with very large batch sizes or multi-GPU/multi-tenant deployment.

The theoretical contribution (Proposition 4.1) establishes distributional properties of rotated subspace vectors but does not provide any formal recall or approximation-error guarantee for the overall coarse-to-fine retrieval pipeline, so the 'high-fidelity' and 'near-lossless' claims rest entirely on empirical results rather than theory.

The relationship to prior rotation-based transformations for quantization (e.g., QuaRot, SpinQuant, cited in Related Work) that similarly use random/learned orthogonal rotations to stabilize distributions is not explicitly discussed or differentiated, leaving some ambiguity about the precise novelty of the rotation trick versus its application to drift-robust retrieval specifically.

Minor inconsistency between reported speedup figures in the abstract (17x/44x) versus the conclusion (17x/44x) is fine, but the introduction's contribution list states 45x for PQCache while abstract and conclusion state 44x, suggesting insufficient proofreading of quantitative claims.
